title: Colombia’s Road to Peace Runs Through the Countryside
gist: A former USAID Colombia deputy mission director argues both Petro’s failed “total peace” negotiations and de la Espriella’s incoming El Salvador-style megaprison agenda miss the real constraint — rural development, the 2016 Peace Accord chapter that is only 9 percent implemented despite consuming 85 percent of the accord’s budgeted cost — and offers the Rural Roads for Total Peace program (856 of 1,035 projects completed in year one, cheaper per kilometer than traditional contracting) as the scalable template.

themes.theme: Policy Whiplash Between Negotiation and Megaprisons

insights.claim: Gustavo Petro’s “total peace” strategy of negotiating with a wide array of criminal and ideological armed groups failed, and incoming Colombian president Abelardo de la Espriella has promised security through law and order including El Salvador-style megaprisons.
insights.speaker: Jeremiah A. Carew
insights.so_what: Colombian security policy is swinging to a Bukele-style incarceration model — relevant to prison construction contracts, coca supply forecasts, and cartel-related sanctions risk.
insights.locator: Conservative outsider Abelardo de la Espriella

insights.claim: Colombia still faces the Ejercito de Liberación Nacional, a longtime ideological guerrilla group that has never signed a peace accord, and the Clan del Golfo cartel, so neither negotiation nor crackdown has removed the armed-group problem.
insights.speaker: Jeremiah A. Carew
insights.so_what: Persistent armed-group control keeps rural Colombia off-limits for formal investment regardless of which security doctrine is in office.
insights.locator: Big swings in the approach to conflict are nothing new

insights.claim: Colombia has repeatedly oscillated between social-justice and law-and-order approaches — Uribe’s hard line, then a FARC peace accord that voters narrowly rejected in 2016 before Congress approved it — and both poles have left large-scale rural development untried in earnest.
insights.speaker: Jeremiah A. Carew
insights.so_what: Betting on either security doctrine ignores the variable that actually determines coca economics and territorial control; watch rural capex, not prison capacity.
insights.locator: The country has shown deep ambivalence

insights.claim: Large-scale rural development would be a game-changer for interrupting the coca-growing economy, bringing state presence and law and order, and increasing private investment into lawless areas of the hemisphere’s most unequal country.
insights.speaker: Jeremiah A. Carew
insights.so_what: Rural road and infrastructure spending is the underpriced lever on Colombian coca supply — a variable that feeds directly into global cocaine volumes and U.S. drug policy.
insights.locator: Left behind in the debate between these two extremes

insights.claim: The Kroc Institute’s May 2026 assessment found the rural development chapter of Colombia’s 2016 Peace Accord has achieved just 9 percent of completion, the least of any of the accord’s six chapters, even though transitional justice and political participation have progressed well.
insights.speaker: Jeremiah A. Carew
insights.so_what: A 9 percent implementation rate on the accord’s largest chapter quantifies the shortfall that will keep driving rural insurgency and coca cultivation.
insights.locator: According to the Kroc Institute’s latest assessment

insights.claim: The rural development chapter is by far the most expensive part of Colombia’s Peace Accord to implement, requiring 85 percent of the accord’s total cost according to the Colombian government.
insights.speaker: Jeremiah A. Carew
insights.so_what: The 85-percent-of-cost versus 9-percent-of-delivery gap is the fiscal scale of the unfunded commitment any Colombian government inherits.
insights.locator: Yet according to the Colombian government

insights.claim: Rural development is the first chapter of the Peace Accord, reflecting its importance to millions in the rural areas where the FARC made its home, and its non-implementation is why one rural woman told the author in 2022 that the accord stayed on paper.
insights.speaker: Jeremiah A. Carew
insights.so_what: Rural credibility of the state is the ground truth behind recruitment into armed groups — the accord’s reputational failure is a live security input.

insights.claim: Urban Colombians commonly refer to rural places as “the territories,” a uniquely Colombian phrasing that is both archaic and binary and reflects a normalized belief that the countryside is poor, backward, and unimprovable.
insights.speaker: Jeremiah A. Carew
insights.so_what: Elite attitudes, not just budgets, explain chronic underinvestment — a structural reason to discount announced rural programs from Bogotá.
insights.locator: Why has rural development been ignored?

insights.claim: Of 1,035 rural road projects started in 2023 under the Petro administration’s Rural Roads for Total Peace program, 856 were completed — an 85 percent success rate for community-led infrastructure that even program critics acknowledged.
insights.speaker: Jeremiah A. Carew
insights.so_what: An 85 percent completion rate is hard evidence that community-led delivery works in fragile settings, contradicting the case for centralized contracting.
insights.locator: Even program critics acknowledged that of 1035 projects

insights.claim: Community-led implementation of Colombian rural roads was cheaper per kilometer than traditional contracting, and very detailed audits found no evidence for the widespread urban-professional belief that country people would steal all the money.
insights.speaker: Jeremiah A. Carew
insights.so_what: The corruption objection that blocks rural spending is empirically wrong — a reason to re-underwrite community-implemented infrastructure across fragile states.
insights.locator: But the program debunked a commonly held belief

insights.claim: The program was designed bottom-up, putting rural communities at the center of decisions so the road section chosen was the right one, communities owned the results, and centuries of paternalism between rural citizens and the state in Bogotá were partly overcome.
insights.speaker: Jeremiah A. Carew
insights.so_what: Local selection authority is the reusable design feature that turns infrastructure spending into state legitimacy, not just asphalt.

insights.claim: The program implemented through existing legally constituted Community Action Boards (Juntas de Acción Comunal) with elected volunteer representatives able to sign contracts with the central government, rather than creating new entities — a deliberate risk reduction in a very legalistic country.
insights.speaker: Jeremiah A. Carew
insights.so_what: Using pre-existing legal vehicles is the transferable trick for scaling rural programs fast without new legislation.
insights.locator: Second, the program leveraged well known

insights.claim: Scaling community-built infrastructure required specific adaptations by Colombia’s roads authority: switching from informal volunteer labor to formal labor contracts for legal liability reasons, and hiring community organizers to help engineers work with communities.
insights.speaker: Jeremiah A. Carew
insights.so_what: These are the concrete cost lines that make community-led delivery replicable rather than a one-off pilot.
insights.locator: Third, the program managers recognized where they lacked experience

themes.theme: Why the Program Broke and What Comes Next

insights.claim: The Rural Roads for Total Peace program fell victim to the fiscal crunch of the Petro administration’s second two years, leaving many accepted communities without roads, and recent reporting alleges it fell apart in year two with too many projects, little funding, too little supervision, and vote-buying schemes led by the Ministry of Finance.
insights.speaker: Jeremiah A. Carew
insights.so_what: Colombia’s fiscal deterioration, not program design, killed the most promising rural initiative — the binding constraint on any successor program is budget headroom.

insights.claim: Colombia’s roads authority professionals were among the most talented and hardworking the author encountered in 25 years of overseas development work, yet were surprisingly unfamiliar with rural development and working with rural people.
insights.speaker: Jeremiah A. Carew
insights.so_what: Institutional capability exists but is misdirected — capacity-building costs for a rural pivot are lower than they appear.
insights.locator: My experience working with the Colombian roads authority

insights.claim: De la Espriella has a clear mandate for law and order, and extending large-scale rural development to the rural places that tended to vote for his opponent is a tried-and-true way to knit Colombia into one peaceful country.
insights.speaker: Jeremiah A. Carew
insights.so_what: Whether the new government pairs megaprisons with rural spending is the single best forward indicator of Colombian security outcomes over his term.
insights.locator: President-elect de la Espriella has a clear mandate
